title: CSRF
body:
Cross-Site Request Forgery abuses the fact that the browser attaches [[Cookies]] **automatically** to every matching request, regardless of which site caused the request. If you're logged into your bank and then visit a malicious page, that page can trigger a request to the bank — a form post, an image tag — and your session cookie rides along. The [[Same-Origin Policy]] stops the attacker from *reading* the response, but the request itself already happened, and if it was a state-changing action, the damage is done.

The core defence is the `SameSite` cookie attribute: `Strict` never sends the cookie on cross-site requests, `Lax` sends it only on top-level navigations with safe methods, `None` sends it always (and requires `Secure`). CSRF tokens — an unguessable value the attacker's page cannot read or predict — are the older complementary defence. Note that [[localStorage]] tokens carry no direct CSRF risk precisely because nothing attaches them automatically; you pay for that with more [[XSS]] exposure instead.
